claim: The inferior colliculus (IC) is the major midbrain auditory integration center, where virtually all ascending auditory inputs converge.
source: The inferior colliculus (IC) is the major midbrain auditory integration center, where virtually all ascending auditory inputs converge.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature establishing this anatomical fact.

claim: Little is known about the neural activity of the IC in moving subjects.
source: Although the IC has been extensively studied for sound processing, little is known about the neural activity of the IC in moving subjects, as frequently happens in natural hearing conditions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, inferred from the literature review.

claim: The activity of IC neurons is strongly modulated by locomotion, even in the absence of sound stimuli.
source: Here, by recording neural activity in walking mice, we show that the activity of IC neurons is strongly modulated by locomotion, even in the absence of sound stimuli.
evidence: Supported by experimental recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar modulation was found in hearing-impaired mice, demonstrating that IC neurons receive non-auditory, locomotion-related neural signals.
source: Similar modulation was also found in hearing-impaired mice, demonstrating that IC neurons receive non-auditory, locomotion-related neural signals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from hearing-impaired mice presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sound-evoked activity was attenuated during locomotion.
source: Sound-evoked activity was attenuated during locomotion, and this attenuation increased frequency selectivity across the neuronal population, while maintaining preferred frequencies.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing sound-evoked responses during stationary and walking conditions.

claim: Attenuation of sound-evoked activity during locomotion increased frequency selectivity across the neuronal population.
source: Sound-evoked activity was attenuated during locomotion, and this attenuation increased frequency selectivity across the neuronal population, while maintaining preferred frequencies.
evidence: Supported by analysis of frequency tuning widths during stationary and walking conditions.

claim: Preferred frequencies were maintained during locomotion despite attenuation of sound-evoked activity.
source: Sound-evoked activity was attenuated during locomotion, and this attenuation increased frequency selectivity across the neuronal population, while maintaining preferred frequencies.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing best frequencies did not change during locomotion.

claim: During behavior, integrating movement-related and auditory information is an essential aspect of sound processing in the IC.
source: Our results suggest that during behavior, integrating movement-related and auditory information is an essential aspect of sound processing in the IC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The IC plays a critical role in representing spectrotemporal features and communication sounds.
source: The IC plays a critical role in representing spectrotemporal features and communication sounds (Egorova et al., 2001; Escabı́ and Schreiner, 2002; Lesica and Grothe, 2008; Woolley and Portfors, 2013), and localizing sound sources (Bock and Webster, 1974; Schnupp and King, 1997; Lesica et al., 2010; Xiong et al., 2013; Ono and Oliver, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The IC plays a critical role in localizing sound sources.
source: The IC plays a critical role in representing spectrotemporal features and communication sounds (Egorova et al., 2001; Escabı́ and Schreiner, 2002; Lesica and Grothe, 2008; Woolley and Portfors, 2013), and localizing sound sources (Bock and Webster, 1974; Schnupp and King, 1997; Lesica et al., 2010; Xiong et al., 2013; Ono and Oliver, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most IC neural activities have been recorded in stationary subjects.
source: While auditory response properties have been extensively studied, most IC neural activities have been recorded in stationary subjects, and little is known about IC activity in subjects engaged in locomotion.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on literature review.

claim: The central nucleus of the IC predominantly receives auditory inputs.
source: The central nucleus of the IC predominantly receives auditory inputs.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The shell region of the IC (the lateral and dorsal cortex) receives non-auditory projections such as somatosensory inputs.
source: However, the shell region of the IC (the lateral and dorsal cortex) receives non-auditory projections such as somatosensory inputs (Cooper and Young, 1976; Morest and Oliver, 1984; Coleman and Clerici, 1987; Lesicko et al., 2016) and performs multi-sensory integration (Aitkin et al., 1978; Aitkin et al., 1981; Jain and Shore, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The shell region of the IC performs multi-sensory integration.
source: However, the shell region of the IC (the lateral and dorsal cortex) receives non-auditory projections such as somatosensory inputs (Cooper and Young, 1976; Morest and Oliver, 1984; Coleman and Clerici, 1987; Lesicko et al., 2016) and performs multi-sensory integration (Aitkin et al., 1978; Aitkin et al., 1981; Jain and Shore, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The shell region of the IC has been implicated in generating sound-driven behavior by projecting to motor-related regions.
source: This region has also been implicated in generating sound-driven behavior by projecting to motor-related regions (Huffman and Henson, 1990; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Modulation of the IC activity during vocalization or eye movements suggests that the main role of non-auditory inputs is to provide motor-related information.
source: Although this multi-modal integration may serve a range of functions (Gruters and Groh, 2012), modulation of the IC activity during vocalization (Schuller, 1979; Tammer et al., 2004) or eye movements (Groh et al., 2001; Porter et al., 2006; Porter et al., 2007) suggests that the main role of non-auditory inputs is to provide motor-related information.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior studies.

claim: It is hypothesized that the auditory system distinguishes self-generated sounds from external ones in order to accurately detect and localize sounds during movement.
source: In order to accurately detect and localize sounds during movement, it is hypothesized that the auditory system distinguishes self-generated sounds from external ones (Poulet and Hedwig, 2002; Rummell et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 2018) and integrates movement-related signals with auditory information.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature.

claim: The auditory system integrates movement-related signals with auditory information.
source: In order to accurately detect and localize sounds during movement, it is hypothesized that the auditory system distinguishes self-generated sounds from external ones (Poulet and Hedwig, 2002; Rummell et al., 2016; Schneider et al., 2018) and integrates movement-related signals with auditory information.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature.

claim: Movements such as locomotion strongly modulate neural activity in the mouse primary auditory cortex (A1).
source: Recent studies in behaving mice show that movements such as locomotion strongly modulate neural activity in the mouse primary auditory cortex (A1) (Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014; McGinley et al., 2015; Bigelow et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A1 neurons receive movement-related signals from sources outside the auditory pathway.
source: While A1 neurons receive movement-related signals from sources outside the auditory pathway (Schneider et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2013; Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Reimer et al., 2016), movement-related modulation is also found in subcortical auditory centers.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Movement-related modulation is found in subcortical auditory centers.
source: While A1 neurons receive movement-related signals from sources outside the auditory pathway (Schneider et al., 2014; Nelson et al., 2013; Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Reimer et al., 2016), movement-related modulation is also found in subcortical auditory centers.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the medial geniculate body (MGB), sound-evoked activity is attenuated during locomotion.
source: In the medial geniculate body (MGB), for instance, sound-evoked activity is attenuated during locomotion (Williamson et al., 2015; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Motor-related modulation is found in the auditory brainstem during vocalization, licking, and pinna orientation.
source: Motor-related modulation is also found in the auditory brainstem during vocalization, licking, and pinna orientation (Suga and Schlegel, 1972; Schuller, 1979; Kanold and Young, 2001; Singla et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Subcortical modulation studies suggest that the integration loci for movement-related and auditory information are spread out along the auditory pathway.
source: These subcortical modulation studies suggest that the integration loci for movement-related and auditory information are spread out along the auditory pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior studies.

claim: Among 96 recorded IC neurons, 51 (53%) significantly increased their firing during locomotion.
source: Among the 96 recorded IC neurons, 51 (Figure 1A; 53%) significantly increased their firing during locomotion, whereas 22 (Figure 1B; 23%) decreased their firing (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among 96 recorded IC neurons, 22 (23%) decreased their firing during locomotion.
source: Among the 96 recorded IC neurons, 51 (Figure 1A; 53%) significantly increased their firing during locomotion, whereas 22 (Figure 1B; 23%) decreased their firing (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In 23 neurons (24%), firing rates did not significantly differ between the stationary and walking periods.
source: In 23 neurons (24%), firing rates did not significantly differ between the stationary and walking periods.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons that increased firing showed a positive correlation between the firing rate and walking speed.
source: Neurons that increased firing showed a positive correlation between the firing rate and walking speed, whereas those that decreased firing showed a negative correlation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons that decreased firing showed a negative correlation between the firing rate and walking speed.
source: Neurons that increased firing showed a positive correlation between the firing rate and walking speed, whereas those that decreased firing showed a negative correlation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anatomical reconstruction of the recording locations did not show any clustering in terms of modulation or the direction of modulation.
source: Anatomical reconstruction of the recording locations did not show any clustering in terms of modulation or the direction of modulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All three types of modulations – increased, decreased, or no change - were found across the IC with no clear pattern.
source: Instead, all three types of modulations – increased (red), decreased (blue), or no change (black) - were found across the IC with no clear pattern.
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When mice walk on a treadmill, their movements generate low-intensity sounds.
source: When mice walk on a treadmill, their movements generate low-intensity sounds.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental setup.

claim: Playbacks of walking sounds evoked neural responses, but the response magnitudes did not significantly correlate with those induced by locomotion.
source: Playbacks evoked neural responses, but the response magnitudes did not significantly correlate with those induced by locomotion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing locomotion-induced and playback-induced responses.

claim: It is unlikely that the modulation is mainly due to auditory reafference.
source: This suggests that although some of the observed modulation may be induced by walking sounds, it is unlikely that the modulation is mainly due to auditory reafference.
evidence: This is an inference based on the playback experiment results.

claim: Firing rate changes can begin well before the onset of locomotion.
source: We found that firing rate changes can begin well before the onset of locomotion (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by locomotion onset-triggered firing-rate averaging data.

claim: In most of the 30 neurons that yielded a significant onset-triggered average, the onset of firing-rate modulation preceded the locomotion onset (median latency = −107 msec).
source: In most of the 30 neurons that yielded a significant onset-triggered average (see Materials and methods), the onset of firing-rate modulation preceded the locomotion onset (Figure 2C, n = 30, median latency = −107 msec).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on modulation timing.

claim: Negative latencies were observed regardless of the direction of the modulation.
source: These negative latencies were observed regardless of the direction of the modulation (Figure 2D; positive modulation: red bar, n = 22, –118 msec; negative modulation: blue bar, n = 8, –60 msec; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p=0.25).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on modulation timing.

claim: Neural modulation can begin before any detectable movement, and is, therefore, not simply an auditory response to walking sounds.
source: This demonstrates that neural modulation can begin before any detectable movement, and is, therefore, not simply an auditory response to walking sounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the negative latency data.

claim: Bilateral deafening by removing the middle ear ossicles and applying an ototoxin (kanamycin) to the cochlea raised the hearing threshold to ≥70 dB, at least 40 dB higher than the threshold in normal mice.
source: Systematic mapping of multi-unit responses to broadband noise across the IC showed that this deafening raised the hearing threshold to ≥70 dB, at least 40 dB higher than the threshold in normal mice (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on hearing thresholds in deafened mice.

claim: In hearing-impaired mice, it would be highly unlikely that low-intensity walking sounds (~30 dB) would evoke neural responses.
source: We reasoned that in these mice, it would be highly unlikely that low-intensity walking sounds (~30 dB, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) would evoke neural responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the elevated hearing thresholds in deafened mice.

claim: Both increases and decreases in neural firing during locomotion were observed in hearing-impaired mice, as in normal-hearing mice.
source: We observed both increases and decreases in neural firing during locomotion in hearing-impaired mice, as in normal-hearing mice (n = 34; Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from hearing-impaired mice.

claim: Modulated neurons were found across the IC without any spatial pattern in hearing-impaired mice.
source: We confirmed anatomically that our recording sites in the hearing-impaired mice were in the IC, and as in normal mice, modulated neurons were found across the IC without any spatial pattern (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by anatomical reconstruction data from hearing-impaired mice.

claim: The existence of locomotion-modulated neurons in hearing-impaired mice with similar characteristics provides strong evidence that non-auditory signals modulate the activity of IC neurons during locomotion.
source: Although we cannot exclude the influence of deafening-induced plasticity, the existence of locomotion-modulated neurons in hearing-impaired mice with similar characteristics provides strong evidence that non-auditory signals modulate the activity of IC neurons during locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the hearing-impaired mouse data.

claim: Most IC neurons with excitatory tone-evoked responses showed significant attenuation during locomotion (72%, n = 47/65).
source: We found that most IC neurons with excitatory tone-evoked responses showed significant attenuation during locomotion (72%, n = 47/65; Figure 4A–C and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on tone-evoked responses during locomotion.

claim: Percent changes in evoked response across the population showed a significant shift toward negative values with a mean change of −36 ± 5%.
source: Percent changes in evoked response across the population showed a significant shift toward negative values (Figure 4H, n = 65; one sample t-test, p=1.4×10−10) with a mean change of −36 ± 5%.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of evoked response data.

claim: Percent attenuation was greater in neurons with relatively weaker responses than in those with stronger responses.
source: Percent attenuation was greater in neurons with relatively weaker responses (below the median) than in those with stronger responses (above the median) (Figure 4I, left; stronger: −17 ± 4%, n = 33; weaker: −56 ± 7%, n = 32; t-test, p=0.0175).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of evoked response data.

claim: For individual neurons, average attenuations at non-best frequencies were greater than those at a neuron's best frequency.
source: For individual neurons, average attenuations at non-best frequencies were greater than those at a neuron's best frequency (Figure 4I, right; n = 43, –27 ± 5% (BF) vs. −48 ± 7% (non-BF); paired t-test, p=6.98×10−4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of evoked response data.

claim: The greater attenuation of weaker responses within and across neurons may improve the signal-to-noise ratio across the neuronal population during locomotion.
source: The greater attenuation of weaker responses within and across neurons may improve the signal-to-noise ratio across the neuronal population during locomotion.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the observed attenuation pattern.

claim: No significant differences in attenuation were found between neurons with onset-only responses and those with sustained responses.
source: We did not find significant differences between the two types (Figure 4J; −45 ± 6% vs. −29 ± 7%; t-test, p=0.103).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of evoked response data.

claim: The degree of attenuation did not correlate with best frequencies, indicating the attenuation was global, rather than frequency-specific.
source: The degree of attenuation also did not correlate with best frequencies, indicating the attenuation was global, rather than frequency-specific (Figure 4K, n = 65; r = −0.0031, p=0.98).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of evoked response data.

claim: During locomotion, there was a significant decrease in the tuning widths across the population (mean change = −0.29 octaves).
source: During locomotion, there was a significant decrease in the tuning widths across the population (Figure 4L–M, n = 60, excluding five neurons with tuning width of 0 during walking due to near-complete suppression; one sample Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=3.0×10−7; mean change = −0.29 octaves).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of frequency tuning data.

claim: Best frequencies did not change during locomotion in the vast majority of the neurons.
source: In contrast, best frequencies did not change during locomotion in the vast majority of the neurons (n = 60, Figure 4N).
evidence: Supported by analysis of best frequency data.

claim: Sound-evoked activity in the IC is attenuated during locomotion, and this attenuation significantly sharpens frequency tuning across the population.
source: Together, these results demonstrate sound-evoked activity in the IC is attenuated during locomotion, and this attenuation significantly sharpens frequency tuning across the population.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Attenuation of evoked activity occurred regardless of spontaneous activity modulation types.
source: Attenuation of evoked activity occurred regardless of spontaneous activity modulation types, but the degree of attenuation correlated with the suppression of spontaneous activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the relationship between spontaneous and evoked activity modulation.

claim: Locomotion-induced suppression of spontaneous and evoked activity may share common neural mechanisms, distinct from excitation.
source: Therefore, locomotion-induced suppression of spontaneous and evoked activity may share common neural mechanisms, distinct from excitation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between spontaneous and evoked activity suppression.

claim: In the sustained type, positive modulation was the most common, whereas in the suppressed type, negative modulation was the most common.
source: In addition, spontaneous modulation differed depending on the evoked response patterns. In the sustained type, positive modulation was the most common, whereas in the suppressed type, negative modulation was the most common (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of the relationship between spontaneous modulation and evoked response patterns.

claim: These correlations suggest an overlap between modulatory and sound-driven inputs, but this overlap is partial.
source: These correlations suggest an overlap between modulatory and sound-driven inputs, but this overlap is partial because the suppressed type can also be excited by locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlations.

claim: Locomotion can modulate spontaneous activity bidirectionally and attenuates sound-evoked activity in the IC.
source: By recording neural activity in the IC of behaving mice, we found that locomotion can modulate spontaneous activity bidirectionally and attenuates sound-evoked activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: Locomotion-related neural signals are robust and wide-spread at this relatively early stage of the auditory pathway.
source: Our results indicate that locomotion-related neural signals are robust and wide-spread at this relatively early stage of the auditory pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The prevalence of movement-related signals suggests that multi-modal integration of movement and sound is an essential part of sound processing in the IC.
source: The prevalence of movement-related signals suggests that multi-modal integration of movement and sound is an essential part of sound processing in the IC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: In the MGB, prior studies reported no changes in spontaneous activity during locomotion.
source: However, in the MGB, the main target of the IC, prior studies reported no such changes in spontaneous activity (Zhou et al., 2014; Williamson et al., 2015; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: One plausible explanation for the discrepancy between IC and MGB spontaneous activity modulation is that the modulation of IC spiking activity primarily evokes subthreshold responses in thalamic neurons.
source: One plausible explanation for this discrepancy is that the modulation of IC spiking activity primarily evokes subthreshold responses in thalamic neurons, making it difficult to detect, but might still modulate sound-evoked activity (Jain and Shore, 2006) in the MGB during locomotion (Williamson et al., 2015; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed differences.

claim: The attenuation observed in the IC could explain in part the similar attenuation observed in the MGB neurons by prior studies.
source: The attenuation observed in the IC could explain in part the similar attenuation observed in the MGB neurons by prior studies.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between IC and MGB findings.

claim: The average decrease in tuning width across the population (~0.3 octaves) was greater than a behaviorally discriminable difference (≤10% or ~0.14–0.15 octaves).
source: The average decrease across the population (~0.3 octaves) was greater than a behaviorally discriminable difference (≤10% or ~0.14–0.15 octaves; Günter, 1975; Clause et al., 2011; de Hoz and Nelken, 2014; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison with behavioral discrimination thresholds from prior literature.

claim: While the attenuation of sound-evoked activity may contribute to poorer tone detection during locomotion, the increase in frequency selectivity may improve frequency discrimination.
source: Thus, while the attenuation of sound-evoked activity may contribute to poorer tone detection during locomotion (McGinley et al., 2015; Schneider et al., 2018), the increase in frequency selectivity may improve frequency discrimination (Aizenberg et al., 2015; Carcea et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional consequences of the observed changes, informed by prior literature.

claim: It is likely that auditory reafference contributes to the observed modulation.
source: It is likely that auditory reafference contributes to the observed modulation, and our results do not exclude contributions of peripheral mechanisms such as bone conduction.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential contributing factor.

claim: The negative modulation latency (~100 msec) and the robust modulation in hearing-impaired mice suggest that central mechanisms play the major role.
source: However, the negative modulation latency (~100 msec) and the robust modulation in hearing-impaired mice suggest that central mechanisms play the major role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing and hearing-impaired mouse data.

claim: One obvious candidate for central mechanisms is the somatosensory inputs to the IC.
source: One obvious candidate is the somatosensory inputs to the IC (Cooper and Young, 1976; Aitkin et al., 1978; Coleman and Clerici, 1987; Zhou and Shore, 2006; Lesicko et al., 2016; Olthof et al., 2019), which may provide feedback during locomotion and modulate sound-evoked activity (Aitkin et al., 1978; Jain and Shore, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation about the source of modulation, informed by prior literature.

claim: Somatosensory projections predominantly target the lateral cortex of the IC.
source: Somatosensory projections predominantly target the lateral cortex of the IC (Lesicko et al., 2016), but we found modulated neurons throughout the IC (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a statement combining prior knowledge with the current findings.

claim: Wide-spread modulation across the IC may occur via connections within the IC, via multi-sensory inputs from the dorsal cochlear nucleus, or via descending inputs from the somatosensory cortex.
source: This may occur via connections within the IC (Rockel and Jones, 1973; Coleman and Clerici, 1987; Jen et al., 2001), via multi-sensory inputs from the dorsal cochlear nucleus (Kanold and Young, 2001; Singla et al., 2017; Goyer et al., 2019), or via descending inputs from the somatosensory cortex (Olthof et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms, informed by prior literature.

claim: Somatosensory signals are more wide-spread across the IC than has been previously hypothesized.
source: Regardless of the precise neural mechanisms, our results suggest that somatosensory signals are more wide-spread across the IC than has been previously hypothesized, and a crucial function of these inputs is providing feedback about ongoing movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: A crucial function of somatosensory inputs to the IC is providing feedback about ongoing movement.
source: Regardless of the precise neural mechanisms, our results suggest that somatosensory signals are more wide-spread across the IC than has been previously hypothesized, and a crucial function of these inputs is providing feedback about ongoing movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The results are compatible with efference copy of motor signals, or movement-related neuromodulatory signals, described in A1.
source: Our results are also compatible with efference copy of motor signals, or movement-related neuromodulatory signals, described in A1 (Nelson et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2014; Nelson and Mooney, 2016; Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms, informed by prior literature.

claim: The IC may receive motor-related signals via the descending projections from the motor cortex.
source: The IC may receive motor-related signals via the descending projections from the motor cortex (Olthof et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms, informed by prior literature.

claim: Cholinergic inputs from the peduncular pontine nucleus, which is part of the midbrain locomotion region, may play a role in locomotion-related modulation.
source: Cholinergic inputs from the peduncular pontine nucleus (Farley et al., 1983; Motts and Schofield, 2009), which is part of the midbrain locomotion region (Lee et al., 2014; Caggiano et al., 2018), and noradrenergic inputs from the locus coeruleus (Klepper and Herbert, 1991; Hormigo et al., 2012), which are active during locomotion (Reimer et al., 2016), may also play a role.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms, informed by prior literature.

claim: Noradrenergic inputs from the locus coeruleus, which are active during locomotion, may play a role in locomotion-related modulation.
source: Cholinergic inputs from the peduncular pontine nucleus (Farley et al., 1983; Motts and Schofield, 2009), which is part of the midbrain locomotion region (Lee et al., 2014; Caggiano et al., 2018), and noradrenergic inputs from the locus coeruleus (Klepper and Herbert, 1991; Hormigo et al., 2012), which are active during locomotion (Reimer et al., 2016), may also play a role.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms, informed by prior literature.

claim: Modulation can differ depending on the response types.
source: Our results indicate that modulation can differ depending on the response types (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of modulation across different response types.

claim: It will be important to determine how locomotion-related signals modulate different cell types such as excitatory, inhibitory, or other specific subtypes.
source: In addition to identifying the sources of modulation, it will be important to determine how these signals modulate different cell types such as excitatory, inhibitory (Ono et al., 2017), or other specific subtypes (Oliver et al., 1994; Ito et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2018; Goyer et al., 2019; Schofield and Beebe, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Neural signals induced by locomotion would inform IC neurons of movement and posture.
source: Neural signals induced by locomotion would inform IC neurons of movement and posture.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of locomotion-related signals.

claim: Movement-related information could be used for distinguishing self-generated sounds from external ones.
source: These movement-related information could then be used for distinguishing self-generated sounds from external ones.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of locomotion-related signals.

claim: Suppression of auditory responses during motor behaviors is hypothesized to prevent desensitization.
source: Suppression of auditory responses during motor behaviors (Creutzfeldt et al., 1989; Eliades and Wang, 2013; Schneider et al., 2014; Singla et al., 2017) is hypothesized to prevent desensitization (Poulet and Hedwig, 2002; Schneider and Mooney, 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature.

claim: Preventing desensitization may be one of the functions of the attenuation observed in the IC, especially in environments where walking makes louder sounds.
source: This may be one of the functions of the attenuation we observed, especially in environments where walking makes louder sounds (Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the observed attenuation.

claim: Movement-related signals in the IC may enable rapid behavioral responses to a sound source by integrating spatial and body information.
source: In addition, movement-related signals in the IC may also enable rapid behavioral responses to a sound source by integrating spatial and body information (Huffman and Henson, 1990; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of movement-related signals, informed by prior literature.

claim: Functions of the IC during behavior are highly multi-modal and integrate sound processing with ongoing behavior.
source: In conclusion, our results suggest that functions of the IC during behavior are highly multi-modal and integrate sound processing with ongoing behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Neural recordings were performed in C57BL/6N mice (n = 15) or a transgenic mouse line (VGAT-ChR2-EYFP line with C57BL/6J background; n = 10) of both sexes, aged 6–10 weeks.
source: Neural recordings were performed in C57BL/6N mice (n = 15) or a transgenic mouse line (VGAT-ChR2-EYFP line with C57BL/6J background in which ChR2-EYFP was targeted to the Slc32a1 gene that encodes VGAT, Jackson Laboratory stock #014548; n = 10) of both sexes, aged 6–10 weeks.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: No differences in the degree of modulation in spontaneous or evoked activity between the two mouse strains were found.
source: In the present study, we did not use transgene expression in the transgenic line. No differences in the degree of modulation in spontaneous or evoked activity between the two strains were found.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental findings.

claim: Pure tone stimuli were presented at 70 dB SPL.
source: Pure tone stimuli with a sampling rate of 400 kHz were generated in MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA), and presented at 70 dB SPL using a D/A converter (PCIe-6343, National Instruments), a power amplifier (#70103, Avisoft, Glienicke/Nordbahn, Germany), and an ultrasonic speaker (Vifa, Avisoft).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: In the stationary condition, the tuning widths ranged from 0.5 to 5 octaves with a mean of 2.2 octaves (n = 65).
source: In the stationary condition, the tuning widths ranged from 0.5 to 5 octaves with a mean of 2.2 octaves (n = 65).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental findings.
